cases.abstract: FlashAttention avoids storing quadratic attention matrices, yet reduced memory traffic alone leaves GPU arithmetic and parallel resources underused. FlashAttention-2 improves execution of exact attention by reducing work outside matrix multiplication and changing how attention tiles are assigned to workers. Its online softmax keeps an unnormalized output until the final division, avoiding repeated normalization on hardware where non-matrix arithmetic is relatively costly. Independent query tiles provide additional thread blocks, while assigning separate query rows to warps removes the forward reduction between warps. The computation remains quadratic, with linear auxiliary storage in sequence length. On an A100 80GB GPU, attention benchmarks spanning sequence lengths from 512 to 16k, with 16k tokens per batch, report 1.7-3.0-fold speedups over FlashAttention and peak throughput up to 230 TFLOPs/s. In complete training of 1.3B- and 2.7B-parameter GPT-style models on eight A100 GPUs, throughput improves by up to 1.3-fold over FlashAttention. Gains are larger at 8k than at 2k context, showing that improved attention execution yields workload-dependent training benefits rather than a uniform application-level speedup.
cases.methods: FlashAttention-2 maintains an unnormalized attention output while processing successive key and value tiles. For each query row, it tracks the largest score seen, the sum of exponentials relative to that maximum, and their weighted sum of values. When a tile raises the maximum, the previous sums are rescaled to the new reference before incorporating the tile. A final division by the accumulated exponential sum recovers the softmax attention output without repeated normalization, reducing relatively expensive non-matrix arithmetic. Independent query tiles also expose thread-block parallelism when batch and head counts are small. Within a block, warps own distinct query rows and share keys and values, so their forward outputs need no inter-warp reduction. The backward pass reconstructs probabilities from saved row-wise log-sum-exp statistics. Larger tiles can reduce transfers, but excessive sizes cause register spilling and substantial slowdown or exceed shared-memory capacity.
cases.results: The end-to-end results show substantially larger benefits at 8k than at 2k context. On eight A100 80GB GPUs, the 1.3B-parameter GPT-style model increases from 189 to 196 TFLOPs/s per GPU at 2k context, but from 170 to 220 at 8k when replacing FlashAttention with FlashAttention-2. For the 2.7B model, the corresponding changes are 189 to 205 and 175 to 225. The roughly 1.3-fold gains at 8k therefore coexist with much smaller gains at 2k: attention-kernel speedups do not transfer proportionally to full training throughput. These values use the paper's model-FLOP convention, which counts attention FLOPs without halving them for causal masking. In the separate attention benchmark, total batch tokens remain fixed at 16k as sequence length grows, and FlashAttention-2 runs at 16k where standard PyTorch attention exhausts memory. The evidence supports better GPU utilization and long-context execution of exact attention, with training benefits that depend on context length.
cases.notes: Retained the supplied draft's exact-attention, kernel-throughput, and training contributions. Abstract and Methods connect delayed normalization to reduced non-matrix arithmetic and query-row ownership to independent forward outputs (Sections 3.1-3.3). Results uses Table 1 to distinguish 8k from 2k training gains; the unhalved causal-attention FLOP convention remains attached. The 230 TFLOPs/s figure is a reported kernel peak, not combined forward/backward throughput. Exactness concerns the mathematical operation, not bitwise identity. H100-specific future optimizations remain excluded.

cases.abstract: Speculative decoding reduces serial target-model calls during autoregressive generation without substituting a cheaper model's output distribution for the target distribution. A small draft model proposes several tokens, and the target evaluates their prefixes in parallel. Proposals undergo a target-to-draft probability test; at the first rejection, sampling from a residual distribution supplies the probability mass missing from accepted proposals. This correction makes the procedure distributionally exact for any draft model, while its speed depends on draft cost and agreement with the target. A runtime analysis relates those quantities to proposal length under independent, identically distributed acceptance rates and unchanged target latency during parallel evaluation. Using existing checkpoints at batch size one on a single TPU-v4, a 77M-parameter T5 draft accelerates the 11B-parameter T5-XXL target relative to standard T5X decoding by 3.4-fold for greedy English-to-German translation and 2.6-fold for standard sampling; summarization gains are 3.1-fold and 2.3-fold, respectively. Larger drafts accept more tokens but deliver smaller speedups. The method exploits available concurrency to reduce walltime at the cost of additional arithmetic, rather than reducing inference computation.
cases.methods: Speculative decoding corrects proposal bias using target and draft distributions p and q adjusted for the chosen sampling rule. It accepts a draft token x with probability min(1,p(x)/q(x)). Accepted proposals contribute mass min(p,q); after rejection, sampling from the normalized positive part of p-q supplies the remaining mass, recovering p exactly. For a draft of gamma tokens, the target evaluates gamma+1 prefixes in parallel, retains proposals until the first rejection, and emits a corrected token there or an additional target token after full acceptance. Each iteration thus produces at least one token. If acceptance rates are independent and identically distributed with mean alpha, expected progress is (1-alpha^(gamma+1))/(1-alpha). Dividing this by 1+gamma*c gives the predicted walltime speedup, where c is the draft-to-target runtime ratio. This timing model additionally requires sufficiently long generations and parallel target evaluations that cost no more time than one evaluation.
cases.results: Greater draft agreement does not necessarily produce faster generation. For greedy English-to-German translation with seven proposals, T5-large achieves mean acceptance of 0.82 but only a 1.7-fold walltime speedup, whereas T5-small accepts 0.75 and reaches 3.4-fold. Both use the same 11B-parameter T5-XXL target, existing checkpoints, batch size one, and a single TPU-v4, so the comparison favors the smaller draft's runtime-acceptance balance rather than acceptance alone. With T5-small, switching from greedy decoding to standard sampling at temperature one lowers translation speedup from 3.4-fold to 2.6-fold and summarization speedup from 3.1-fold to 2.3-fold. Acceleration therefore depends on the sampling rule as well as draft choice. These gains reduce walltime, not arithmetic: rejected continuations waste computation, and additional parallel capacity is required. The GPT-like and LaMDA experiments measure acceptance rates rather than generation latency, so they assess draft agreement without extending the demonstrated T5 speedups to those models.
cases.notes: Retained distributional correctness and measured T5 walltime acceleration as separate contributions. Methods makes the accepted probability mass and residual correction explicit (Section 2.3), while the speedup expression retains the assumptions of Sections 3.1 and 3.3. Results compares equal proposal lengths under greedy translation (Table 2), showing why acceptance alone cannot select the fastest draft. The guarantee concerns distributions, not matching individual sampled sequences. GPT-like and LaMDA results remain acceptance measurements, not latency evidence. Adaptive proposal counts, beam search, and non-text uses are not established results.
